response.evidence: By my manual tally, which is approximate, Hispanic or Latino women made up about 110-120 applications, of which roughly 10 were denied (about 8-10%). That is in line with the overall denial rate of about 9-10% and with the rates for Hispanic men (about 9%), White applicants and Asian applicants. The denials in this group mostly coincide with high debt-to-income ratios (47-49, 50%-60%, >60%) or very high loan-to-value ratios (90-97%+), which also led to denials for White, Asian, Black and male applicants. Similar profiles were approved for other groups, so the data show no consistent pattern of denial specific to Hispanic or Latino women. This is a descriptive summary without statistical testing, and the sample is small, so it cannot rule out discrimination.

I counted by hand, so these figures are approximate. Hispanic or Latino women were denied at roughly 12-14% (about 15 denials among about 110-120 applications). The overall denial rate is roughly 9-10%, and the rates for White and Asian women appear lower, around 7%. That is a raw gap, but the data do not show it is caused by discrimination. Many of the denied Hispanic female applicants had very high debt-to-income ratios (50-60% or >60%) or high loan-to-value ratios (95-100%), which are common denial factors across all groups. Hispanic applicants as a group also tend to have higher loan-to-value ratios. Other applicants with similar high ratios were approved, including some Hispanic women. This is not a controlled comparison, and the sample is small and uneven, so the data suggest a disparity but do not establish discrimination.

By my approximate hand count (not an exact tally), Hispanic or Latino women were denied in about 7% of their applications (roughly 8 denials among over 100 applications). The overall denial rate is about 9-10%. White, Asian and Hispanic male and joint applicants have similar denial rates of about 5-10%. The denials of Hispanic or Latino women mostly involve high debt-to-income ratios (over 50%), high loan-to-value ratios (90-97%), or both, and the same factors appear in denials of other groups. The data shows no clear disparity against this group. This is only a descriptive comparison with no statistical testing, and the subgroup is small, so the result is not conclusive.

By my rough hand count (not an exact tally), Hispanic or Latino females make up about 100 applications, with about 14 denied (roughly 13-14%). The overall denial rate looks like roughly 10-12%. Several other groups, including White, Asian, and Black or African American applicants, have similar or higher denial rates. Most denials of Hispanic or Latino women have very high debt-to-income ratios (50-60% or over 60%), zero or very low income, or loan-to-value ratios near or above 95-100%. These factors drive denials for every group. The few denials at moderate debt-to-income ratios, such as 45-48%, are not enough to show a pattern, and the data has no controls for credit score or other underwriting factors. So the data shows no clear evidence of discrimination against Hispanic or Latino women, though the small sample and missing variables limit how certain this is.

Most of the Hispanic female denials also involve high debt-to-income ratios (50%-60% or >60%), very high loan-to-value ratios, or zero or low income. The summary has no formal statistical test and omits credit scores and other underwriting factors, so a hidden disparity cannot be ruled out. That is why my confidence is moderate.

It has no controls for credit score or other factors and no significance testing, so it cannot rule out individual or unmeasured discrimination.
